title: Inheritance
summary: One class reusing another's shape and behavior. Learn base vs derived, overriding, the diamond problem, and when to reach for composition instead.

blocks.markdown:
**Inheritance** lets one class reuse and extend another's fields and methods, instead of copying them.

- The relationship is **"is-a"** — a `Dog` **is a** `Animal`.
- The reused class is the **base** (parent); the reusing one is the **derived** (child).
- A child can **override** a method to change its behavior.
- Overused, it creates rigid hierarchies — [composition](object-relationships) is often safer.

blocks.subTitle: Why it exists
blocks.markdown:
Without inheritance, every similar class repeats the same fields and methods.

- A `Car` and a `Truck` both need `speed`, `start()`, `stop()`.
- A shared `Vehicle` base class holds that once; each child adds only what differs.
- This is **code reuse through hierarchy**, not copy-paste.

The **base class** (also called parent or superclass) defines common fields and methods. The **derived class** (child or subclass) inherits them and adds or changes behavior.

- A derived class automatically gets every non-private member of its base.
- It can add new fields/methods, or **override** inherited ones.
- Only test with "is-a": if it doesn't read naturally, don't inherit.

blocks.subTitle: Method overriding
blocks.markdown:
**Overriding** is when a derived class redefines a method it inherited, using the same name and signature, to give it different behavior.

- The child's version runs instead of the parent's when called on a child object.
- This is what lets one call site work differently per subtype — the basis of [polymorphism](polymorphism).
- Not to confuse with **overloading**: same name, different parameters, no inheritance needed.

blocks.subTitle: Calling super
blocks.markdown:
**super** (or **base**, depending on language) is a reference a derived class uses to call its parent's version of a method or constructor.

- Common use: override a method but still run the original logic first — `super.method()` then add extra steps.
- Constructors often call `super(...)` to let the base class set up its own fields before the child adds its own.

A base class and a subclass overriding one method, in pseudocode:

```text
class Animal:
    field name

    constructor(name):
        this.name = name

    method makeSound():
        print(name + " makes a sound")

class Dog extends Animal:
    constructor(name):
        super(name)          // reuse Animal's setup

    method makeSound():        // override
        print(name + " barks")

// usage
a = new Animal("Generic")
d = new Dog("Rex")
a.makeSound()   // "Generic makes a sound"
d.makeSound()   // "Rex barks" — overridden version runs
```

`Dog` reused `name` and the constructor logic, and only replaced `makeSound()`.

blocks.subTitle: Single & multilevel
blocks.markdown:
Two of the simplest shapes:

- **Single** — one child, one direct parent. `Dog extends Animal`.
- **Multilevel** — a chain: a class inherits from a class that itself inherits from another. `Puppy extends Dog extends Animal`.

Both stay easy to reason about since each class has exactly one parent.

blocks.subTitle: Hierarchical
blocks.markdown:
**Hierarchical inheritance** is one base class with several independent children.

- `Animal` as base; `Dog`, `Cat`, `Bird` each extend it separately.
- Each sibling shares the base's members but knows nothing about the others.
- This is the most common shape in real codebases.

blocks.subTitle: Multiple & the diamond problem
blocks.markdown:
**Multiple inheritance** is one class inheriting from two or more base classes at once.

- Problem: if both bases define the same method, which version does the child get? This ambiguity is the **diamond problem** (named for the diamond-shaped class diagram).
- Many languages (Java, C#) ban multiple class inheritance to avoid it, allowing it only for interfaces, which carry no conflicting implementation.
- C++ allows it but requires explicit rules to resolve the conflict.

How the four shapes differ at a glance.

The diamond shape in (4) is exactly why the diamond problem gets its name.

**Composition** is a **"has-a"** relationship: a class holds another class as a field instead of extending it.

- A `Car` **has an** `Engine` — it stores an `Engine` object and calls its methods, rather than becoming one.
- Composition builds behavior by **combining objects**; inheritance builds it by **extending a type**.
- Both are valid — the question is which one fits the relationship you actually have.

blocks.subTitle: Side by side
blocks.markdown:
| | Inheritance (is-a) | Composition (has-a) |
|---|---|---|
| Coupling | Tight — child depends on parent internals | Loose — only depends on an interface |
| Flexibility | Fixed at compile time | Swap the held object at runtime |
| Best for | True type hierarchies | Reusing behavior across unrelated types |

blocks.subTitle: Favor composition
blocks.markdown:
**"Favor composition over inheritance"** is a well-known design guideline, not an absolute rule.

- Inheritance locks in a relationship at compile time and exposes the parent's internals to every child — change the base and every subclass can break.
- Composition lets you swap the held object, mix behaviors freely, and change things at runtime.
- Use inheritance only for a genuine, stable "is-a"; reach for composition for everything else. See [design-principles](design-principles).

When inheritance is the wrong tool:

- **Forcing an "is-a" that isn't true.** A `Square extends Rectangle` breaks if `Rectangle` allows independent width/height changes — not a real is-a.
- **Deep chains.** Five levels of subclassing make behavior hard to trace; a bug could live in any ancestor.
- **Reusing code, not modeling a type.** If you only want a method from another class, compose it — don't inherit just to borrow logic.

blocks.subTitle: Inheritance vs composition
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Inheritance vs composition — which do you prefer and why?**

Composition, by default. It couples classes loosely — you depend on a small interface, not a parent's internals — and lets you change behavior at runtime by swapping the held object. Inheritance is still right for a genuine, stable "is-a" with shared behavior that won't fight the hierarchy later.

blocks.subTitle: The diamond problem
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the diamond problem?**

When a class inherits from two base classes that share a common ancestor (or the same method), the compiler can't tell which inherited version to use — the class hierarchy literally forms a diamond. Java and C# sidestep it by disallowing multiple class inheritance and using interfaces instead; C++ allows it but needs explicit resolution.

blocks.subTitle: is-a vs has-a
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How do you decide between is-a and has-a?**

Say the sentence out loud. "A Car is a Vehicle" reads naturally — inheritance. "A Car is an Engine" doesn't — but "A Car has an Engine" does, so that's composition. If the sentence needs forcing, it's the wrong relationship.

blocks.subTitle: What super does
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What does calling super() actually do?**

It invokes the parent class's constructor or method from within the child. In a constructor, it's usually the first line — it lets the base class initialize its own fields before the child sets up its additions. In an overridden method, it lets you extend the parent's behavior instead of fully replacing it.

blocks.subTitle: When inheritance is a bad choice
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Give an example where inheritance was the wrong choice.**

The classic one: `Square extends Rectangle`. `Rectangle` lets width and height change independently; forcing `Square` to keep them equal breaks that contract — code that resizes a `Rectangle` can silently corrupt a `Square`. The fix is composition or a shared interface, not a forced is-a.

blocks.subTitle: Overriding vs overloading
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What's the difference between overriding and overloading?**

**Overriding** needs inheritance: a subclass redefines a method with the exact same signature to change its behavior, resolved at runtime. **Overloading** needs no inheritance: multiple methods share a name but differ in parameters, resolved at compile time.
